description.value: The study investigated relationships between childhood family stress and neural responses to threatening emotional faces, including amygdala and right ventrolateral prefrontal cortex activity and their connectivity, using functional magnetic resonance imaging.

spans.text: The present study sought to investigate these neural mechanisms by examining the relationship between a risky family environment and neural responses to emotional stimuli, as assessed by functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).

value: Thus, we predicted that offspring from risky families would reveal deficits in threat detection abilities and in the regulation of responses to potentially threatening stimuli, as evidenced in amygdala and RVLPFC responses to threat-relevant tasks.

description.value: A nonclinical cross-sectional study of 30 healthy participants who completed a risky family assessment followed two to six weeks later by fMRI tasks involving observation, emotion labeling, and gender labeling of negative emotional faces.

instructions.value: Participants completed observe-only, emotion-labeling, and gender-labeling blocks. They were instructed to observe the face without responding in the observe-only condition, choose the correct emotion label (fear or anger) in the emotion-labeling condition, and choose the gender-appropriate name in the gender-labeling condition. They were told to respond as soon as they were sure of the correct answer.

stimuli.value: Target faces displaying negative emotional expressions, specifically fearful or angry faces, presented for 5-second trials. Emotion-labeling trials displayed the labels fear and anger; gender-labeling trials displayed pairs of gender-appropriate names; observe-only trials displayed the face without response options.
